title: Marco Rubio and the Myth of the “Communist Refugee”
author: Nick Estes
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-20-at-1.24.08-PM.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/21/marco-
rubio-and-the-myth-of-the-communist-refugee/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-20-at-1.24.08-PM.png)

Marco Rubio, image by Wikipedia.

Fox News host Martha MacCallum recently interviewed New York City Democratic
Socialists of America (DSA) co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, clashing over whether
the DSA’s platform is “anti-American” and challenging Gordillo’s immigrant
roots. MacCallum reminded Gordillo that his family left Peru, suggesting their
reasons might be related to the communist uprising led by the Shining Path and
not, as Gordillo claims, related to U.S. imperialism. MacCallum contrasted
this by discussing Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Cuban immigrant family’s
embrace of American capitalism, weaponizing it against Gordillo’s embrace of
socialist policies. She then played a clip of Rubio’s opening remarks at the
recent Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism, where he
attempted to debunk the myth that communism sounds good in theory but is bad
in practice.

“Communism does not sound good in theory,” Rubio said. “The world it envisions
for all of us is small, flat, grey, leveled of all exception, drained of all
that is good and noble in the human soul.”

Is that so? Let's subject that claim to the cold light of historical reality.

By framing the debate around these two men, MacCallum tried to push the
classic “good immigrant versus the bad immigrant” trope. The underlying
implication is that, just like Rubio’s family, Gordillo’s fled communist
violence. This sets up a neat, right-wing rhetorical trap: how can ostensible
“victims of communism” oppose capitalism, the very system that supposedly
saved them? However, a look at actual history obliterates this narrative: the
truth is that neither Rubio’s nor Gordillo’s families fled communism at all.

According to Gustavo Gordillo, his family fled Peru because of U.S.
imperialism and neoliberal policies—that is, capitalist disaster, not
communist uprising. Instead of escaping Marxism, they left their home in the
1990s during a wave of aggressive, U.S.-backed economic “shock therapy” that
resulted in the fire-sale selling off of public services and crushing
hyperinflation. At the time, the CIA funneled millions of dollars to Peruvian
intelligence agencies, ostensibly for anti-narcotics operations. In reality,
U.S. intelligence agencies were fully aware that Peruvian intelligence and
military officials used these resources to operate brutal, state-sanctioned
death squads against groups they claimed were communist “terrorists”—a label
weaponized against many Indigenous communities, regardless of their actual
political alignments. Gordillo’s family was displaced by the violent fallout
of capitalist extraction, not socialist policy; they were refugees of a brutal
“free market” experiment backed by death squads, not the Shining Path.

Marco Rubio’s family, on the other hand, left Cuba in 1956—immigrating to the
United States a full three years before Fidel Castro, the leader of the Cuban
Revolution, ever took power. Throughout his years in politics, Rubio has
consistently embellished his family story, even claiming to be the “son of
exiles.” He frequently called Castro a “thug” for forcing Cuban Americans,
like his parents, off their beloved island. However, his entire career in far-
right politics has been built on this fabricated myth that his parents fled
the Cuban Revolution, a fiction calculated to bolster his strident anti-Castro
and anticommunist bona fides among the so-called Cuban “exile” community in
Southern Florida.

The historical reality is that his family left Cuba during the reign of
Fulgencio Batista—a brutal, U.S.-backed dictator. Ironically, it was same
regime that targeted fellow anticommunist and anti-Castro fanatic, Texas
Senator Ted Cruz’s father, who was beaten for opposing the Batista regime and
later obtained political asylum in the United States. During this era, the
United States backed Batista’s suppression of political dissent to protect
corporate profits. Pre-revolutionary Cuba functioned essentially as an
American corporate playground: American corporations controlled nearly all of
Cuba’s nickel and mineral exports and owned nearly all of its electric and
phone services. Furthermore, the infamous United Fruit Company owned 40
percent of the sugar production and three-quarters of the island’s arable
lands. When the Cuban Revolution finally took power, it nationalized and
expropriated these exploitative corporate industries, redistributing their
wealth back to the Cubans themselves.

In short, Rubio’s parents didn’t flee the revolution—they fled the oppressive
corporate extraction that made the revolution necessary in the eyes of many.

Now, we come to the ultimate historical irony. Rubio wants to reintroduce the
very system of extraction and plunder back to his parents’ homeland that
likely led to their initial departure in the first place. He wants to make
Cuba “great again” by returning it to its prior state of pupilage under the
American boot. This glaring hypocrisy is abundantly clear in his fanatical
obsession with overthrowing the government of Cuba and his recent histrionics
around how Cuba has sponsored leftist movements in the United States.
Ultimately, corporate media uses the “communist refugee” myth not out of
empathy for people fleeing violence, but as an ideological shield to protect
Western imperialism from critique.

empathy for people fleeing violence, but as an ideological shield to protect
Western imperialism from critique. And in the case of Rubio, it shows how
capitalism in theory and in practice is a world made of awesome violence and
propaganda, where even its ostensible victims are systematically hollowed out
until they become its most strident, genocidal defenders.
